title: The exosome prion chain
claim: Prion-bearing extracellular vesicles transmit disease to animals.
subject: Prions
stage_note: trace complete; 8/8 verified at source. The hypothesis is open, not the trace: the claim as worded depends on vesicle enclosure, which Entry 011 records as untested.
plain_status: Material from the preparation called exosomes causes disease when injected into the brains of PrP-overexpressing mice, in two independent studies. Whether that material is carried inside vesicles, rather than as free aggregate pelleting alongside them, has not been established.
summary: 8-node trace, all verified at source. The pellet transmits; whether the infectivity is inside the vesicles is an open question (Entry 011).
lede: One claim, traced link by link through its citations — with the exact sentence at each step and how well each one can be verified. The honest result: on reading the sources, the core claim holds, with narrower caveats than the downstream language suggests.
author: Priority Nexus LLC

blocks.text: Four different claims get substituted for one another in this literature. Keeping them apart is what makes the drift visible.

items.text: **T1** The protein is **present in** a vesicle preparation.
**T2** It **transfers between cultured cells**, with a readout in the recipient.
**T3** It **seeds aggregation in an animal** after inoculation.
**T4** It **transmits clinical disease to an animal**, with an attack rate.

blocks.text: The claim above is a **T4** claim. Février 2004 and Vella 2007 both report **T4** results (intracerebral bioassays, different groups and strains); the other readable papers report **T1 or T2** work.
Verification reflects checks on 6 October 2026: all eight nodes confirmed against the publishers' own pages, full text read for each.

nodes.heading: Origin — an exosome bioassay in mice
nodes.citation: Février B, Vilette D, Archer F, Loew D, Faigle W, Vidal M, Laude H, Raposo G. "Cells release prions in association with exosomes." *Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A.* 2004;101(26):9683–9688. [doi:10.1073/pnas.0308413101](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0308413101)
nodes.quote: "we found that exosomes bearing PrPsc are infectious."

details.label: What it shows
details.text: An intracerebral bioassay (Table 1): the 100,000 × g exosome pellet from scrapie-infected Rov cells — and that fraction purified on a sucrose gradient — injected into tg338 mice (overexpress ovine PrP), strain 127. Pellet 5/5, 76.8 ± 2.6 days; purified fraction 5/5, 78 ± 1.2 days; diluent control 0/5, >200 days.

details.label: What it does not show
details.text: Transmission by any route other than injection into the brain, or in mice with normal PrP levels.

details.label: Note
details.text: Independent of Vella 2007 (different group, different strain) and concordant with it — two separate demonstrations of the same claim.

details.label: Files
details.text: Full text read 6 Oct 2026.

nodes.heading: The in-vivo experiment — read at source
nodes.citation: Vella LJ, Sharples RA, Lawson VA, Masters CL, Cappai R, Hill AF. "Packaging of prions into exosomes is associated with a novel pathway of PrP processing." *Journal of Pathology* 2007;211(5):582–590. [doi:10.1002/path.2145](https://doi.org/10.1002/path.2145)
nodes.quote: "these exosomes produced prion disease when inoculated into mice."

details.label: What it shows
details.text: An intracerebral bioassay (Table 1): material from M1000-infected moRK13 and GT1-7 cells injected into Tga20 mice, which overexpress mouse PrP. Infected exosomes — 5/5 mice developed disease, mean incubation 90–98 days. Non-infected controls — 0/3 and 0/4, no disease past 300–370 days.

details.label: What it does not show
details.text: Transmission by any route other than injection into the brain, or in mice with normal PrP levels; and how the exosomes' infectivity compares with brain tissue (no titration). Concordant with Février 2004 — an independent demonstration, different group and strain.

details.label: Cites
details.text: Février 2004 and others, for the vesicle association.

details.label: Files
details.text: Full text read 6 Oct 2026.

nodes.heading: A third reference, often bundled with the first two
nodes.citation: Alais S, Simoes S, Baas D, Lehmann S, Raposo G, Darlix JL, Leblanc P. "Mouse neuroblastoma cells release prion infectivity associated with exosomal vesicles." *Biology of the Cell* 2008;100(10):603–615. [doi:10.1042/bc20080025](https://doi.org/10.1042/bc20080025)
nodes.quote: "The dissemination of prions in N2a cell culture is mediated through the exosomal pathway."

details.label: What it shows
details.text: Cell-culture only: scrapie-infected N2a neuroblastoma cells release exosome-associated infectivity that transfers to target N2a cells. No animal experiment — confirms the T2 tier. The earlier "three identities" conflict was resolved by reading it.

details.label: Cites
details.text: Février 2004, for the vesicle association.

details.label: Files
details.text: Full text read 6 Oct 2026.

nodes.heading: Bundling — three references, one claim, two tiers
nodes.citation: Bellingham SA, Guo BB, Coleman BM, Hill AF. "Exosomes: vehicles for the transfer of toxic proteins associated with neurodegenerative diseases?" *Frontiers in Physiology* 2012;3:124.
nodes.quote: "Both PrP<sup>C</sup> and PrP<sup>Sc</sup> have been isolated in association with exosomes, and PrP<sup>Sc</sup> containing exosomes were infectious in both animal and cell bioassays."

details.label: Cites
details.text: Février 2004; Vella 2007; Alais 2008 — all three behind the single phrase "animal and cell bioassays."

details.label: What happens
details.text: Three references across two evidence tiers merge into one claim, with no indication which reference supplies the animal tier. Hill is an author of both this review and Vella 2007.

details.label: Files
details.text: — none attached

nodes.heading: The paper that will be miscited — cell culture only
nodes.citation: Guo BB, Bellingham SA, Hill AF. "Stimulating the release of exosomes increases the intercellular transfer of prions." *J. Biol. Chem.* 2016;291(10):5128–5137.
nodes.quote: "Treatment of the prion-infected MoRK13 donor cells with increasing amounts of MON results in a corresponding increase in the amount of PrP<sup>Sc</sup> detected in the recipient cells."

details.label: Systems
details.text: MoRK13, GT1-7, A2 and RK13 cell lines. Transwell assays, PMCA, microscopy.

details.label: Animals
details.text: **None.** No in-vivo experiment anywhere. Its own Discussion calls for "comprehensive in vivo analyses" as future work.

details.label: Files
details.text: — none attached

nodes.heading: The miscitation — tier inflation by citation
nodes.citation: Hartmann A, Muth C, Dabrowski O, Krasemann S, Glatzel M. "Exosomes and the prion protein: more than one truth." *Frontiers in Neuroscience* 2017;11:194.
nodes.quote: "Pharmacological stimulation of exosome release by treatment with the ionophore Monensin increased release of infectious exosomes. Moreover, exosomes isolated from these *in vitro* experiments were able to transmit prion disease *in vivo*."

details.label: Cites
details.text: Guo 2016 (ref 25) — the cell-culture-only paper above — for the in-vivo claim.

details.label: Also in it
details.text: The same paper attributes the in-vivo claim correctly to Vella 2007 elsewhere, and cites Cervenakova 2016 for animal transmission. A different lab from Guo's, so the error is independent, which is what lets it propagate.

details.label: Cited ref
details.text: Cervenakova et al. 2016, "Are prions transported by plasma exosomes?" (*Transfusion and Apheresis Science*) — a secondary reference cited here, not one of the chain's eight nodes. Identity confirmed via Crossref; paywalled, so not read in full.

details.label: Files
details.text: — none attached

nodes.heading: Propagation, and apparent independent support
nodes.tier: Two refs, one unreadable + one miscited
nodes.citation: Zheng T, Pu J, Chen Y, et al. "Plasma exosomes spread and cluster around β-amyloid plaques in an animal model of Alzheimer's disease." *Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience* 2017;9:12.
nodes.quote: "The exosomes from human-derived prions infected cells are efficient initiators of prion propagation in uninfected recipient cells and produce clinical prion disease when inoculated into mice."

details.label: Cites
details.text: Vella 2007 and Guo 2016 together — the unreadable source paired with the miscited one.

details.label: Why it matters
details.text: The claim now appears to rest on two independent papers. A reader who checks the first and finds support stops there. And this is an Alzheimer's paper — the claim is now background in a field where no prion specialist is reviewing it.

details.label: Files
details.text: — none attached

nodes.citation: Soukup J, Moško T, Kereïche S, Holada K. "Large extracellular vesicles transfer more prions and infect cell culture better than small extracellular vesicles." *Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications* 2023;687:149208. [doi:10.1016/j.bbrc.2023.149208](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbrc.2023.149208) · first posted as bioRxiv [10.1101/2023.03.01.530593](https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.03.01.530593)
nodes.quote: Cell-culture only: CAD5 and N2a-PK1 prion cell-culture models, comparing large versus small vesicles. It keeps "in cell culture" in its own title, and it cites Février, Vella, Guo, Alais and Cervenakova — Vella specifically for infection "both in vitro and in vivo". An earlier version of this entry said the paper declined to cite those authors; reading the reference list on 12 October 2026 showed that was wrong, and the inference drawn from it has been withdrawn.

blocks.text: Traced expecting citation drift. The transmission evidence held up: two independent primary studies show the preparation causes disease. What did not hold is the wording. The claim says "extracellular vesicles", and nothing in the chain establishes that the infectious material is inside the vesicles rather than free aggregate pelleting with them — see [[011-prion-infectivity-inside-extracellular-vesicles|Entry 011]].

items: **The transmission is supported; the wording is not.** Février 2004 and Vella 2007 — different groups, different prion strains — each show material from the preparation causes disease when injected into the brains of PrP-overexpressing mice. Whether that material is vesicle-enclosed is a separate, open question. The chain is not built on an unverifiable source.

**But the scope is narrow.** Both use the most permissive assay: intracerebral injection into mice that overexpress PrP. Downstream text repeats "transmit to animals" without that scope, so the claim reads broader than what was shown.

**One citation points to the wrong paper.** Hartmann 2017 cites Guo 2016 — a cell-culture-only study — for the in-vivo claim. The claim is true, but Guo is not where it was shown; the correct sources are Février and Vella. (Hartmann also cites Vella correctly elsewhere.)

**Tiers get bundled.** The 2012 review merges references spanning cell-culture and animal work into one phrase ("animal and cell bioassays"), so a reader cannot tell which reference supports which tier.

items.text: **Established.** Two independent studies — Février 2004 (sheep strain) and Vella 2007 (human-derived strain), different groups — show that material from the ~100,000 × g pellet of infected-cell medium causes disease when injected into the brains of PrP-overexpressing mice (both 5/5; ~77 and ~90–98 days; clean controls).

**Not established: that the pellet's infectivity is carried inside vesicles.** The pellet contains free prion aggregate as well as vesicles, and the protease-protection test normally used to show enclosure cannot distinguish them for this protein. Février's sucrose-gradient fraction transmitted 5/5, which answers part of the objection; it does not establish enclosure. This claim as stated therefore rests on an open question — see [[011-prion-infectivity-inside-vesicles|Entry 011]].
**Still open.** Both demonstrations use the most permissive assay. These are the tests that would extend the claim beyond it.

blocks.text: All eight nodes are verified at source as of 6 October 2026 — the full text of each was read. One cautionary note from the process: while assembling an earlier draft, an automated reader returned a confidently formatted citation for the 2008 reference that gave a wrong title and journal — the same failure this map documents. Reading the paper resolved it.
